We hired eleven people last year. I interviewed most of them, and I got at least three wrong.
Looking back, the pattern is obvious. I over-weighted confidence and under-weighted curiosity. The people who interviewed best weren't always the people who worked best.
No slides. No brainteasers. Just real work.
It's slower. It's more expensive. And it's the best hiring decision we've made.

I'm 41 and I wrote my first working script on Saturday. It renames files. That's all it does.
It took four hours, most of them spent on an error that turned out to be a missing bracket. The AI assistant found it in one go once I thought to paste the whole file instead of describing it badly.
I don't think this makes me a developer. I do think I understand my engineering colleagues about ten percent better, which was worth the Saturday.
Next up is something that renames files and also moves them. Ambitious.

It sounds simple. In practice, it's anything but. Many teams track activity, such as logins and prompts sent, rather than outcomes. Others rely on anecdotes. Few have a clear baseline to compare against.

I started using AI to take meeting notes three months ago. The results surprised me.
The notes themselves were fine. What changed was how I showed up in meetings. I stopped typing and started listening. I asked better questions. I noticed when someone went quiet.
It turns out the value wasn't in the transcript. It was in the attention I got back.

Someone is copying numbers between three files every Monday, and it takes them half a day. They've heard AI can fix it.

Sometimes it can. More often the fix is a lookup formula and a shared folder, and nobody needs a model at all. I've started asking one question before anything else: what would you do with the time? If the answer is vague, the project usually dies in a month.
The Monday copying is rarely the real complaint anyway. It's that nobody trusts the numbers once they've been copied.
At the end of the month, we'll gather feedback to see whether the change has improved productivity, reduced distractions, and helped us manage our workloads more effectively.
How to Give Feedback That Actually Helps Your Colleagues
Whether you're addressing a missed deadline, recognizing excellent work, or suggesting a better approach, the way you communicate can make all the difference.

Useful feedback isn't about pointing out mistakes or telling someone what they're doing wrong. It's about helping colleagues understand their strengths, identify opportunities to improve, and feel confident about their next steps.
The key is to focus on specific examples, choose the right moment, and approach every conversation with respect.
